## Amos 7 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

### Overview of the Chapter

The chapter falls into two sections: three visions of judgment (vv. 1–9) and a historical confrontation between Amos and Amaziah, the priest of Bethel (vv. 10–17). The visions escalate: locusts, fire, then a plumb line — the first two judgments are averted by the prophet’s intercession; the third is final and irreversible.

---

### v. 1 — “He was preparing swarms of locusts just after the king’s harvest, as the late spring crop was coming up.”

**Traditional reading:** God showed Amos a vision of a locust swarm forming at the worst possible time — after the king had taken the first cutting of hay or crops (likely for his cavalry and court), so what remained belonged to the people. If locusts devoured that second growth, the people would be destitute until the next year’s harvest. The vision uses an agricultural calamity known from Joel and the curses of Deuteronomy 28:38–42 as a figure of divine judgment.

- David Guzik (Enduring Word): “If the first cutting went to the court and the second crop to the locusts, Israel would be left destitute indeed” (citing Hubbard). The royal tax came first; the locusts claimed the rest. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-7/]
- Constable: The spring crops harvested later fed the people and their animals. “If anything happened to prevent that second harvesting, the people would have little to eat until the next harvest in the fall.” Locust swarms were a perennial threat and a covenant curse (Deut 28:38, 42). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-7.html]
- Utley: “This would have been sometime after April. The later rain had to occur before the seeds would sprout. If this crop was lost there would be no crop until the next year!” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/amos-7.html]
- Ellicott: “Amos saw the first wave of disaster in the destruction of the food of the people.” [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/7.htm]
- Calvin (Reformed): He understood the locusts metaphorically as “hostile invasions, which had not immediately laid waste the whole country but in some measure desolated it” — a moderate punishment compared to what follows. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/amos-7.html]
- Pulpit Commentary: “No agents are too insignificant for the employment of Jehovah. He can inflict terrible judgments by insects.” [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/amos/7.htm]

---

### v. 2 — “Lord GOD, please forgive! How will Jacob survive, since he is so small?”

**Traditional reading:** Amos intercedes with a plea for forgiveness, not just for the judgment to stop. He appeals to God using the covenant name “Jacob” — reminding God of the patriarch who was the younger, weaker brother, and of the nation’s frailty.

- Guzik: “Israel is called Jacob, a reminder that he was the smaller, younger one to Esau in Isaac’s family; God had deliberately chosen him and therefore was obligated to stand by him in his helplessness” (citing Hubbard). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-7/]
- Constable: “Amos’ view of Israel as small and weak stands in contrast to that of Israel’s leaders who believed it was strong and invincible.” Under Jeroboam II, Israel had its second-largest territory ever, “but it was still small in relation to the larger empires.” God had promised to care for Jacob at Bethel (Gen 28:10–22) — now a centre of apostate worship. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-7.html]
- Calvin: Amos prays for pardon because “there is nothing that inclines God more to mercy than the recollection of his gratuitous covenant.” He notes the prophet appeals not to Israel’s worthiness but to her weakness: “he calls him small, because he had been worn out by many calamities.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/amos-7.html]
- Utley: The prophet appeals to the nation’s “need,” not to their covenant relationship. “The Lord had promised that Abraham’s seed would be as the stars … the sand … the dust of the earth, but now there were so few!” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/amos-7.html]
- Ellicott: The cry literally means “Who is Jacob that he should stand? for he is small.” [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/7.htm]

---

### v. 3 — “So the LORD relented from this plan. ‘It will not happen,’ He said.”

**Traditional reading:** The prayer of a righteous person avails much. God responds to intercession; this is an anthropomorphism — God accommodates Himself to human language.

- Guzik: “What if Amos had not prayed, or if he had not prayed with the same earnestness? The sense of this passage is that the LORD would not have relented.” This raises profound questions about prayer and God’s will. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-7/]
- Utley: The Hebrew root means “to breathe heavy” — it expresses deep feeling. “God is often spoken of in the Bible as changing His mind or relenting … God is affected by our prayers and His character of compassion and love. However, this should not be understood in the sense that God’s nature or purpose vacillates. It does not change (cf. Num 23:19; 1 Sam 15:29; Mal 3:6).” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/amos-7.html]
- Calvin: “God changes not his purpose so as to retract what he has once determined … but he accommodates himself to the measure of men’s understanding, when he mentions such changes.” The eternal purpose was always to threaten, show tokens of displeasure, yet suspend vengeance. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/amos-7.html]
- Gill (Baptist): “He did not change his mind, but changed the dispensations of his providence according to his mind and will.” [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/7.htm]
- Constable: “Some things that God intends to do are not firmly determined by Him; He is open to changing His mind about these things. However, He has decreed other things and no amount of praying will change His mind.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-7.html]

**Denominational note — Reformed:** Calvin insists God’s decree never changes; the “relenting” language is accommodation to human comprehension. Constable (Dallas Seminary/Evangelical) makes a distinction between decreed and negotiable aspects of God’s will. Both are careful to preserve divine sovereignty.

---

### v. 4 — “The Lord GOD was calling for judgment by fire. It consumed the great deep and devoured the land.”

**Traditional reading:** The second vision is more severe than the first. Fire represents a more terrifying judgment — perhaps a scorching drought that dries up even the subterranean waters (“the great deep”). The language of a legal “contention” or “lawsuit” is present.

- Guzik: “Amos saw a vision of a great consuming fire upon the land of Israel.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-7/]
- Constable: “Like a great drought it consumed all the water and all the farmland … So intense was the fire that Amos saw that it dried up even these underground water reservoirs.” This was another covenant curse (Deut 28:22). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-7.html]
- Ellicott: “The poetical description of a yet more terrible calamity … The consuming of the ‘great deep’ is a strong hyperbole.” The image is of a prairie fire eating up what the locusts spared. Not only pasture but “the deepest springs of moisture” would be scorched. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/7.htm]
- Utley: The term translated “contend” refers to a legal case — “a divorce case, e.g., Hosea 4:1; 12:2; Micah 6:1–2.” Fire is a common symbol of judgment; in this agricultural context it may refer to scorching heat. The “great deep” refers to “the underground water source of rivers … a mythological term from Sumer and Babylon, but in the OT it has been totally stripped of its mythological connotation.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/amos-7.html]
- Calvin (Reformed): God, seeing that common remedies (locusts) did not heal the people, doubled the punishment. “The Lord’s usual mode of proceeding … At first he tries … and applies not the most grievous punishment, but such as may be endured; but when he perceives hardness and obstinacy, he doubles and trebles the punishment.” The phrase “called to contend” indirectly condemns the people’s hardness — “as when no justice can be obtained, a litigation becomes necessary.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/amos-7.html]

---

### vv. 5–6 — “Lord GOD, please stop! … So the LORD relented … ‘It will not happen either.’”

**Traditional reading:** Amos prays again, but this time says “stop” (or “cease”) rather than “forgive.” The judgment is averted once more, but a subtle shift in language may hint that the nation’s guilt is deepening and forgiveness is harder to ask for.

- Guzik: “In response, he did what he did before: he pled for mercy … As happened with the vision of locusts, God relented at the prayer of the prophet.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-7/]
- Ellicott: “Instead of ‘forgive,’ the prophet now only ventures to say ‘cease,’ a cry for arrest of judgment. Yet the same plea for pity is urged as before. Jeroboam II and his house are spared for awhile. But another awful vision comes.” [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/7.htm]
- Utley: “This time the prophet did not appeal for forgiveness, but for the cessation of judgment. YHWH is merciful, but there is an end to His patience (cf. Amos 7:8; 8:1).” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/amos-7.html]

---

### v. 7 — “Behold, the Lord was standing by a wall true to plumb, with a plumb line in His hand.”

**Traditional reading:** The third vision introduces a different symbol. A plumb line is a builder’s tool — a cord with a weight used to test whether a wall is perfectly vertical. The wall represents Israel, originally built “true to plumb” by God. Now God stands with the plumb line to test, and this time there will be no passing over.

- Guzik: “A plumb line measures if a wall is built straight. God held this measure against Israel, to see if they were straight against His standard.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-7/]
- Calvin (Reformed): He refuses to allegorise the plumb line excessively (“frigid are almost all their refinements”). The simple meaning: “this would be the last measuring; for he would punish his people without any remission and without any delay.” God had twice “leaped over the bounds of his judgment by sparing them,” but now the final end has come. The wall is that “which had been formed by rule” — Israel was built well, but now is to be measured for demolition. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/amos-7.html]
- Constable: “The wall was probably a city wall … A plumb line was a string with a weight on the end. People used it … to determine if a vertical structure is completely straight. God was testing something by a true standard; His judgment is not arbitrary.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-7.html]
- Ellicott: “Wall made by a plumbline — i.e., a perpendicular wall, the stability of the kingdom being represented by the closely-fitting well-jointed stones of a lofty wall.” He notes that the plumb line was used both for building and for marking out destruction (cf. 2 Kings 21:13; Isa 34:11). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/7.htm]
- Utley notes an alternative view: the rare Hebrew word may actually mean “tin” (an Akkadian loan word), not “plumb line.” If so, the imagery would be of a “tin wall” — a metaphor of weak, apparent protection. Most English translations, however, accept “plumb line.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/amos-7.html]
- Preacher’s Complete Homiletical Commentary: “God, the builder of the nation, tests and finds it degenerate … The hand which builds our families and estates can destroy them, if we deviate from rectitude.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/amos-7.html]

---

### v. 8 — “I am setting a plumb line among My people Israel; I will no longer spare them.”

**Traditional reading:** This is the turning point of the visions. God will no longer “pass by” (spare) them. Israel has been measured against God’s standard — probably the Mosaic Law — and found crooked beyond remedy. Amos notably does not intercede this time; he understands that the time for mercy has passed.

- Guzik: “Because Israel was chronically crooked against the plumb line of God, Israel and her leadership would be judged with the sword.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-7/]
- Constable: “The true standard by which He would judge Israel was undoubtedly the Mosaic Law … The Lord further announced that He would not spare the Israelites from His judgment any longer; Amos’ prayers for Israel would not turn away His punishment … The nation was so far out of plumb that God would tear it down.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-7.html]
- Ellicott: “‘Pass by them’ — in the sense of sparing. There will come a time when prayer will be of no avail. All intercessions, however passionate or eager, will be too late. The door of mercy is shut.” [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/7.htm]
- Utley: “Literally ‘I will never again pass by them.’ Amos realizes the depth of Israel’s rebellion and ceases to intercede on her behalf.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/amos-7.html]
- Calvin (Reformed): “I fix this to be the last rule, or the final measure … ‘I will proceed no farther in forgiving them: as when a wall is formed to the plumbline, that no part may, in the least, exceed another, but that there may be regularity throughout so also this shall be the last order; this measuring shall be true and just.’” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/amos-7.html]

---

### v. 9 — “The high places of Isaac will be deserted, and the sanctuaries of Israel will be laid waste; and I will rise up against the house of Jeroboam with My sword.”

**Traditional reading:** All centres of worship — both the local “high places” and the national shrines at Dan and Bethel — will be destroyed. “The house of Jeroboam” refers to the dynasty of Jeroboam II (or the kingdom established by Jeroboam I). The method of judgment shifts from locusts and fire to the sword (invading army).

- Guzik notes that “Isaac” here is unusual — “the only places in the Old Testament where Isaac stands for the nation of his descendants rather than for the patriarch himself” (citing Hubbard). It may reflect special northern veneration for Isaac through pilgrimages to Beersheba (Amos 5:5; 8:14). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-7/]
- Constable: “This enemy, as Yahweh’s agent, would destroy the outdoor high places on hilltops and the temple sanctuaries at Dan and Bethel.” Jeroboam II’s dynasty ended with the assassination of his son Zechariah (2 Kings 15:8–10). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-7.html]
- Calvin (Reformed): The people “in vain trusted in their temples and superstitions, for by these they kindled the more against themselves the wrath of God.” Why “Isaac”? Calvin speculates it may be a deliberate corruption of the spelling (using shin instead of tsade) to show contempt for the northerners’ false claims to Isaac’s legacy — or that they used “Isaac” flatteringly of themselves. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/amos-7.html]
- Utley: “‘High places’ refer to the local fertility worship sites … ‘sanctuaries’ refer to the national shrines at Dan and Bethel, started by Jeroboam I (922 B.C.).” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/amos-7.html]

---

### vv. 10–11 — Amaziah’s accusation: “Amos has conspired against you … Jeroboam will die by the sword, and Israel will surely go into exile.”

**Traditional reading:** Amaziah, the chief priest at the royal sanctuary of Bethel, sends a distorted report to King Jeroboam II. He frames Amos’s prophecy as political treason. He slightly misquotes Amos (Amos had said God would rise against the *house* of Jeroboam, not that Jeroboam personally would die by the sword), personalising the threat to incite the king.

- Guzik: “This Amaziah was a wicked man because he was identified as a priest of Bethel, which was one of the centers of Israel’s idolatrous worship.” He “implicated the prophet in a conspiracy.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-7/]
- Constable: “By claiming that Amos was predicting Jeroboam’s death, the priest was personalizing the danger of Amos’ ministry to the king and was emotionally inciting him to take action … Amaziah regarded Amos’ prophecies as simply the prophet’s own words. He had no respect for them as messages from Israel’s God.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-7.html]
- Utley: “Amaziah accused Amos of political treason … Near Eastern kings were very conscious of their prophet’s words and popularity among the populace and feared any negative prediction.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/amos-7.html]

---

### vv. 12–13 — “Go away, you seer! Flee to the land of Judah … never prophesy at Bethel again, because it is the sanctuary of the king.”

**Traditional reading:** Amaziah tries to expel Amos. Calling him a “seer” may be disparaging. He tells Amos to “eat bread” (earn a living) in Judah — implying Amos is only prophesying for money. Bethel is described as the “king’s sanctuary” and “temple of the kingdom” — revealing that Amaziah sees it as a state institution, not God’s house.

- Guzik: “Amaziah was offended that Amos came to Bethel and prophesied, so he did his best to send him back to Judah.” He cites Adam Clarke: “Hireling priests of this kind have ever been the great enemies of the true prophets of God.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-7/]
- Constable: “By telling him to eat (earn) his bread in Judah, he was hinting that Amos needed to get a ‘legitimate’ job rather than living off the contributions he received for prophesying … Bethel, of all places, was an inappropriate town in which Amos should utter messages of doom against Israel, from Amaziah’s perspective.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-7.html]
- Utley: “It is obvious that Amaziah was expressing the truth ironically when he states this is not God’s sanctuary but the king’s.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/amos-7.html]

---

### vv. 14–15 — “I was not a prophet … I was a herdsman and a tender of sycamore-fig trees. But the LORD took me … ‘Go, prophesy to My people Israel.’”

**Traditional reading:** Amos’s remarkable self-defence. He denies being a professional prophet or coming from a prophetic guild (“son of a prophet”). He was a shepherd and a cultivator of sycamore figs — a man with his own livelihood who did not need to prophesy for money. God sovereignly called him away from his flocks to deliver an unpopular message. His authority is divine commissioning, not human credentials.

- Guzik: “Amos replied to Amaziah by noting that he was a reluctant, unprofessional prophet … Amos was hardly the type to launch a conspiracy.” He cites Spurgeon: “Every prophet has a manner and style peculiarly his own … The breath which causes the music is the same, but no two of the instruments give forth precisely the same sound.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-7/]
- Constable: “Amos replied that he was not a prophet by his own choosing; he did not decide to pursue prophesying as a career … Amos had a respectable agricultural business background before he moved to Israel to prophesy.” A “nipper of sycamore figs” pierced the fruit so insects could escape and the fruit would become edible (Driver), or slit the fig before ripening to make it sweet (Niehaus). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-7.html]
- Utley: The verb “took” has “a strong theological connotation of God’s sovereign choice and action (e.g., Exod 6:7; Deut 4:20, 34; 2 Sam 7:8).” Amos may be contrasting “prophet” (individual calling) with “son of a prophet” (member of a prophetic group). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/amos-7.html]
- Ellicott: “There is no hint of any lack of education or refinement through the exclusion of any special aid derived from the training of earlier prophets. In this case God’s inward call had been more than sufficient.” [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/7.htm]

**Lutheran reading (1517.org):** The article emphasises that Amaziah treated Amos’s words as merely human words, not God’s Word — “making it Amos’ words, not God’s Word. Amaziah does not believe Amos has been sent by the LORD. So, it is the word of a human being against the Word of God. That is an age-old conflict.” (Retrieved from search excerpt; full page inaccessible.) [https://www.1517.org/articles/old-testament-amos-77-15-pentecost-8-series-b-2024]

---

### v. 16 — “Now, therefore, hear the word of the LORD. You say: ‘Do not prophesy against Israel; do not preach against the house of Isaac.’”

**Traditional reading:** Amos turns from defending himself to delivering a fresh oracle from God directly against Amaziah. He characterises Amaziah’s command as forbidding God’s own word — the ultimate offence.

- Guzik: This is the preamble to the judgment oracle. Amaziah tried to silence the very word that would now pronounce his doom. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-7/]
- Constable: “Preaching” is from the Hebrew verb *natap*, meaning “drip” — as the heavens drip rain (Judg 5:4; Amos 9:13). “The idea is that Amos should stop raining down messages from heaven on his hearers.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-7.html]
- Utley: “This is Amos characterizing Amaziah’s words, which were opposite of YHWH’s.” “House of Isaac” is unique in the OT — “a disparaging comment by Amaziah about Amos’ preaching in the north.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/amos-7.html]

---

### v. 17 — Judgment on Amaziah’s household: wife a prostitute, children slain, land divided, death in a pagan land, Israel exiled.

**Traditional reading:** The judgment pronounced on Amaziah is brutally specific and deeply ironic. The very exile Amaziah tried to silence is now promised to fall on his own family. Each element carries a particular sting for a priest: his wife violated, his children killed (ending his priestly line), his land divided among foreigners, and he himself dying in an “unclean” (pagan) land where he cannot pass on his priestly inheritance.

- Guzik: “God’s word to Amaziah … was that the calamity he wanted to silence Amos about would certainly come upon him … This was a difficult word in most difficult circumstances, but Amos was faithful to deliver it.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-7/]
- Constable: “Stifling the word of God proved disastrous for Amaziah, as it still does today. Finally, Amos repeated that Israel would indeed go into exile, the message that Amaziah had reported that Amos was preaching.” Amaziah’s loyalty was to Jeroboam who appointed him; Amos’s loyalty was to God who sent him. “Primary loyalty to God … would have eliminated conflict between the king, the priest, and the prophet.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-7.html]
- Utley: The judgments mean “neither he nor his descendants would be priests. (1) Wife will be unfit for marriage to a priest (cf. Deut 22:23–24). (2) No children will survive him. (3) He dies in a foreign land unable to pass on his priestly credentials” (citing Hubbard). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/amos-7.html]
- Ellicott: “This doom on Amaziah’s wife is to be regarded as the hideous consequence of war. She shall be ravished. By the polluted land we are to understand Assyria, or the land of exile; for food eaten in any other land than Canaan, the land of Jehovah, was regarded as unclean.” [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/7.htm]

---

### Where Protestant Traditions Differ

1. **God’s “relenting” (vv. 3, 6) and divine immutability:** Reformed teachers (Calvin) stress that God’s eternal decree never changes and the “relenting” language is anthropomorphic accommodation. Arminian-influenced traditions (Methodist, Pentecostal, many Baptists) tend to read the passage more straightforwardly — that prayer genuinely affects God’s actions in history. Constable (Evangelical/DTS) bridges this by distinguishing between what God has decreed unchangeably and what He leaves open to influence by prayer. [Calvin: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/amos-7.html; Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-7.html]

2. **The plumb line as Law vs. finality of judgment:** Calvin explicitly rejects elaborate allegorising of the plumb line as “the law” — he takes it simply as the final, exact measuring for destruction. Other Protestant commentators (Constable, Preacher’s Homiletical Commentary) explicitly identify the plumb line as the Mosaic Law, the covenant standard. Both understandings lead to the same conclusion: Israel failed the test. [Calvin: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/amos-7.html; Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-7.html]

3. **Amos and the prophetic office (v. 14):** Baptist and evangelical readers emphasise Amos as a layman called directly by God without institutional mediation — a pattern for all believers’ calling. Lutheran readers (1517.org) emphasise the Word-of-God vs. word-of-man conflict. Reformed readers (Calvin) highlight God’s sovereign “taking” of Amos from his flock as an act of election parallel to His taking Israel from Egypt. The Pentecostal/charismatic tradition (Guzik/Enduring Word) notes how God used Amos’s agricultural background rather than erasing it — the Spirit works through human individuality. [Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-7/; Calvin: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/amos-7.html]

---

### Other Views

**Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes / text-critical):** Not directly accessible from the searches; however, Utley notes the debated translation of the rare Hebrew word for “plumb line” (*’anak*) — some argue for “tin” based on an Akkadian cognate, which would make the vision one of a weak tin wall rather than a measuring line. Most translations and commentaries retain “plumb line.” [Utley: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/amos-7.html]

**Catholic and Orthodox readings:** Specific Catholic or Orthodox commentary on Amos 7 was not retrievable from the permitted sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org) in the available searches. The Catholic Encyclopedia at newadvent.org contains general articles on Amos but no verse-by-verse treatment of chapter 7 was found.

**Prosperity / Word of Faith / Hyper-Grace readings:** No content from these traditions regarding Amos 7 was found on the sites searched.
